Total gross cost for 1,413 premium requests was \$56.52.
GitHub applied \$28.16 in billing credits (49.8\% effective discount),
yielding a total net developer cost of \$28.36 for a full
production-quality, 20,814-LOC, multi-component toolkit over 30 calendar
days.

Two development phases are visible.
The \emph{intensive sprint} (February~6--11) accounts for 911 requests
(64.5\% of total) and \$25.00 of net cost, during which the VS~Code
extension, web platform foundation, and shared library layer were built
simultaneously.
The \emph{organic tail} (February~12--March~7) covers 502 requests at
\$3.36 net, dominated by documentation, testing, paper preparation, and
post-release maintenance.
The sharp drop in net cost after February~18 reflects account-level
billing credits that covered usage through the end of the study period.

These figures demonstrate that AI-assisted development at the individual
practitioner level is economically accessible: context-aware tooling
directly enables cost efficiency by monitoring token budgets and closing
low-relevance tabs before each request.
The 49.8\% effective discount here reflects GitHub's account-level credits,
not in-session optimisation; instrumented studies comparing token-budget-aware
vs.\ unaware workflows remain a priority for future work
(Section~\ref{sec:future}).


\subsection{Broader Impact}
\label{sec:broader-impact}

\textit{(i) Cost optimization without the mathematics.}
The web platform turns economic theory into nine interactive tools that
any developer can use.
Break-even analysis, Cobb--Douglas optimisation, and conversation cost
projection are each reduced to a form and a chart.

\textit{(ii) Educational resources.}
The 10-lesson context engineering course at
\url{https://tokalator.wiki/learn} progresses from token basics to
production compaction patterns.
The automated wiki aggregates articles from arXiv, OpenAI Cookbook,
Anthropic documentation, and Google AI docs on a bi-monthly schedule.
The dictionary defines 41 terms across seven categories, contributing to
vocabulary standardisation in a field where terminology remains
inconsistent~\citep{burnham2025context}.

\textit{(iii) Ecosystem contribution.}
The catalog of 146+ agents, 140+ prompts, and 161+ instruction files,
auto-discovered from \texttt{copilot-contribution/} and
\texttt{user-content/}, provides a structured starting point for teams
adopting context engineering practices.
The MCP server enables any Claude Code user to access real BPE token
counts without an API key or network call~\citep{anthropic2026claudecode}.
Tokalator's context management practices are also published as a reusable
agent skill installable via \texttt{npx skills add vfaraji89/tokalator}
(\url{https://skills.sh}), making the token budget workflow available to
any agent supporting the Agent Skills specification.

\textit{(iv) Marketplace adoption.}
The VS~Code extension was published on February~4, 2026.
v3.1.3, released March~2026, resolves four field-reported bugs and adds
automatic Copilot model synchronization.
Within its first 30 days (February~4 -- March~8, 2026), it recorded
163~total acquisitions (installs and downloads combined) from 210~page
views, yielding a 77.62\% page-to-acquisition conversion rate
(Table~\ref{executabelMetadata}).
%% [I5] Unified to 163/77.62% — demo file figures (matches current state).
Of the 163 acquisitions, 19 are organic direct installs --- developers
who discovered the extension independently without referral links.
Activity peaked around February~8--14, coinciding with the most intensive
development period (46 commits on February~8) when the extension was
promoted across internal and community channels.
Combined with the 220+ developers reached through community sessions,
these figures indicate genuine practitioner demand for context budget
tooling.

    24→\section{Discussion}
    25→\label{sec:discussion}
    26→
    27→\subsection{Interpretation of Results}
    28→
    29→The three research questions share a common finding: token budget
    30→consumption in AI-assisted development is large, invisible by default,
    31→and highly manageable once made visible.
    32→The 21.2\% context reduction in Example~1 came entirely from removing
    33→files the developer had not intentionally included as context --- they
    34→were simply open tabs accumulated across a working session.
    35→Similarly, the 88.9\% daily cost saving in Example~2 was available to
    36→any team using a 50K-token system prompt, but only became actionable when
    37→the break-even calculation was presented concretely.
    38→These results suggest that the primary barrier to context efficiency is
    39→not developer motivation but information availability.
    40→
    41→The survey results reinforce this: 82\% of respondents named
    42→\texttt{/preview} as their most-valued feature, not because it changes
    43→what the model sees, but because it makes the cost of the next turn
    44→observable before it is incurred.
    45→This aligns with the broader literature on decision support systems:
    46→making a cost function explicit and real-time tends to shift behaviour
    47→even without enforcement~\citep{bergemann2025economics}.
    48→
    49→The model synchronization issue (64\% of users affected) highlights a
    50→structural gap in how current AI coding tools expose their state:
    51→developers switch models in the Copilot UI without any notification to
    52→companion tools.
    53→Tokalator's v3.1.3 auto-sync addresses this at the extension level, but a
    54→standard API for broadcasting active model changes across IDE extensions
    55→would benefit the entire ecosystem.
    56→
    57→\subsection{Practical Implications}
    58→
    59→For development teams adopting AI coding assistants, this work suggests
    60→four actionable guidelines.
    61→
    62→\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
    63→  \item \textit{Audit instruction files first.}
    64→    A \texttt{CLAUDE.md} or \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md}
    65→    file is injected silently into every prompt.
    66→    A 4,000-token instruction file costs the same as 4,000 tokens of
    67→    source code but applies to every single request.
    68→    Teams should treat instruction files as high-ROI targets for context
    69→    reduction.
    70→
    71→  \item \textit{Enable prompt caching for any system prompt used more
    72→    than twice per day.}
    73→    The break-even point for Anthropic models is two reuses.
    74→    For OpenAI's automatic caching, the mechanism is always-on.
    75→    Any team running a chatbot or agent with a fixed system prompt is
    76→    leaving savings unused by not caching.
    77→
    78→  \item \textit{Use sliding-window or summarize strategies for
    79→    conversations longer than 20 turns.}
    80→    Full-history cost grows quadratically; switching to a 5-turn sliding
    81→    window triples the number of affordable turns within the same daily
    82→    budget (28 vs.\ 83 turns in Example~3).
    83→
    84→  \item \textit{Close distractor tabs before starting a coding session.}
    85→    Configuration files (\texttt{.json}, \texttt{.yml}) open alongside
    86→    active source files contribute tokens without providing useful context
    87→    for most coding tasks.
    88→    Running \texttt{@tokalator /optimize} at session start is a low-effort
    89→    habit that reduces per-request cost immediately.
    90→\end{enumerate}
    91→
    92→\subsection{Threats to Validity}
    93→
    94→\textit{Internal validity.}
    95→The relevance score weights ($w_\mathrm{lang}=0.25$,
    96→$w_\mathrm{import}=0.30$, $w_\mathrm{path}=0.20$,
    97→$w_\mathrm{recency}=0.15$, $w_\mathrm{diag}=0.10$) were set by design
    98→reasoning, not measured against data.
    99→One source of bias is that the developer who chose the weights also
   100→observed the study participants, which may have skewed the evaluation.
   101→Future work should tune these weights against a held-out set of human
   102→relevance judgments.
   103→
   104→\textit{Construct validity.}
   105→The extension estimates context consumption from open tabs, but the actual
   106→context construction of GitHub Copilot and Claude Code is proprietary.
   107→The extension's token count is an upper-bound proxy, not a direct
   108→measurement.
   109→All reported figures (e.g., the 21.2\% reduction) reflect estimated
   110→consumption, not confirmed API-level context size.
   111→
   112→\textit{External validity.}
   113→The user study ran at three venues: Kariyer.net internal ($n \approx 50$),
   114→SaaS Bridge ($n \approx 90$), and TechCareer ($n \approx 80$), totalling
   115→$N > 220$ developers.
   116→The internal group shared a TypeScript/React stack; the community sessions
   117→had a wider mix of languages and roles.
   118→The results may not carry over to teams using compiled languages (C++,
   119→Rust), non-web domains, or different working styles.
   120→The sample is sufficient for recurring-feedback triangulation but not
   121→for statistical generalisation.
   122→
   123→\textit{Reliability.}
   124→The Cobb--Douglas sensitivity parameters ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$)
   125→are placeholder values satisfying structural constraints
   126→($\alpha + \beta + \gamma < 1$) but not calibrated from empirical data.
   127→Users relying on the Economic Analysis tool for investment decisions
   128→should treat its outputs as directional guidance, not precise predictions.
   129→
   130→\subsection{Methodological Assumptions}
   131→
   132→The system design rests on several assumptions that should be stated
   133→explicitly.
   134→
   135→\textit{(A1) Open tabs approximate context.}
   136→Tokalator counts tokens from open tabs and adds fixed overheads for system
   137→prompts, instructions, and conversation history.
   138→The actual context construction of GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and
   139→Cursor is proprietary; these tools may include additional signals (git
   140→diffs, terminal output, recently visited files) or exclude files the
   141→extension counts as open.
   142→Estimates are therefore upper-bound approximations, not exact context
   143→measurements.
   144→
   145→\textit{(A2) Five signals suffice for relevance.}
   146→The scorer uses five syntactic signals (Equation~2), assuming that
   147→structural signals --- language match, import relationships, path
   148→similarity, recency, and diagnostics --- capture the most important
   149→dimensions of tab relevance.
   150→Semantically related files without import links will be missed
   151→(Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
   152→The ablation study (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}) quantifies how much each
   153→signal contributes.
   154→%% [I7] Confirmed \ref{sec:rq2} (not \\ref) — bug fixed.
   155→
   156→\textit{(A3) Fixed scoring weights.}
   157→The weights ($w_\text{lang} = 0.25$, $w_\text{import} = 0.30$,
   158→$w_\text{path} = 0.20$, $w_\text{recency} = 0.15$,
   159→$w_\text{diag} = 0.10$) are design-time constants based on domain
   160→reasoning, not learned from data.
   161→Optimal weights likely vary by programming language, project structure,
   162→and developer habits.
   163→The planned ground-truth evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}) will provide
   164→the first empirical basis for calibration.
   165→
   166→\textit{(A4) Cobb--Douglas functional form.}
   167→The economic analysis assumes output quality follows a Cobb--Douglas
   168→production function of input, output, and cached tokens (Equation~5).
   169→While this form captures diminishing returns and substitutability,
   170→actual LLM quality may depend on additional factors (prompt structure,
   171→retrieval accuracy, task decomposition) not representable in a simple
   172→production function.
   173→
   174→\textit{(A5) Pricing stability.}
   175→The calculators use snapshot pricing hardcoded in
   176→\texttt{lib/providers.ts}.
   177→LLM pricing is volatile --- \citet{cottier2025price} documented rapid
   178→declines --- and the tool's outputs are only as current as the last
   179→manual pricing update.
   180→
   181→\subsection{Domain Extension}
   182→
   183→While this paper focuses on AI coding assistants in VS~Code, the core
   184→principles --- context budget decomposition, relevance scoring, and cost
   185→projection --- apply wherever LLM context windows are a constrained
   186→resource.
   187→
   188→\textit{Enterprise knowledge systems.}
   189→RAG pipelines face the same trade-off: retrieved documents consume context
   190→tokens, and irrelevant retrievals dilute model attention.
   191→A relevance scorer analogous to Algorithm~\ref{alg:scoring}, adapted to
   192→score retrieved passages instead of IDE tabs, could help RAG systems
   193→prioritize context quality over quantity.
   194→
   195→\textit{Multi-agent orchestration.}
   196→In multi-agent architectures~\citep{zhu2025onecontext}, each sub-agent
   197→receives a portion of the context budget.
   198→Tokalator's budget decomposition (Equation~1) could extend to per-agent
   199→allocations, enabling orchestrators to detect agents that consume
   200→disproportionate context without proportionate contribution.
   201→
   202→\textit{Non-IDE editors.}
   203→The \texttt{tokalator-mcp} server and CLI already provide IDE-agnostic
   204→token counting.
   205→Adapting the relevance scorer to JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, or browser-based
   206→editors would require only an editor-specific adapter for tab and
   207→diagnostic APIs; the scoring logic (Algorithm~\ref{alg:scoring}) is
   208→platform-independent, as demonstrated by the pure-function extraction
   209→(\texttt{tabRelevanceScorer.pure.ts}).
   210→
   211→
   212→\section{Limitations}
   213→\label{sec:limitations}
   214→
   215→\textit{(i) Approximate tokenization for Google models.}
   216→The extension uses a heuristic of approximately 4 characters per token
   217→for Gemini models, as Google does not provide a client-side BPE tokenizer
   218→for JavaScript.
   219→Anthropic and OpenAI models use actual BPE tokenizers
   220→(\texttt{@anthropic-ai/tokenizer} and \texttt{js-tiktoken} o200k\_base).
   221→We estimate a mean absolute error of 10--15\% on English code and
   222→15--32\% on non-Latin scripts such as Turkish or Arabic, based on
   223→informal comparison with Google's server-side \texttt{countTokens} API
   224→on a sample of TypeScript, Python, and Markdown files.
   225→This limitation is disclosed in the extension dashboard via the tokenizer
   226→label and in Section~\ref{sec:description}.
   227→
   228→\textit{(ii) Provider-update fragility.}
   229→Tokalator's token estimates rest on reverse-engineered assumptions about
   230→how GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Cursor construct their context
   231→payloads.
   232→If any provider silently changes their context-building logic --- which
   233→is entirely proprietary --- Tokalator's overhead constants
   234→($T_{\text{sys}}$, $T_{\text{instr}}$, $T_{\text{out}}$) may become
   235→inaccurate without any visible signal to the user.
   236→Similarly, if a provider changes their tokenizer vocabulary, the BPE
   237→counts emitted by \texttt{@anthropic-ai/tokenizer} or
   238→\texttt{js-tiktoken} may diverge from server-side counts.
   239→Users should verify that token estimates remain reasonable by
   240→spot-checking against API-reported values after major provider releases.
   241→%% [R15] Provider-update fragility added as new limitation per reviewer.
   242→
   243→\textit{(iii) Extension performance overhead.}
   244→The extension subscribes to six VS~Code event streams (active editor,
   245→tab changes, document edits, open/close, diagnostics, configuration).
   246→All handlers use a 300\,ms debounce timer, capping snapshot rebuilds at
   247→$\sim$3 per second.
   248→Token counts are cached per (URI, version); re-tokenisation occurs only
   249→when content changes.
   250→BPE tokenizers are lazy-loaded ($\sim$100--200\,ms one-time on first
   251→activation) and $O(1)$ thereafter.
   252→In informal testing with 30+~open tabs, the extension contributes
   253→$<$5\,ms per snapshot build after warm-up --- imperceptible to the user.
   254→
   255→\textit{(iv) Syntactic rather than semantic relevance.}
   256→The tab relevance scorer (Equation~2) uses structural signals --- import
   257→graphs, path similarity, language match, edit recency, and diagnostics ---
   258→not semantic understanding.
   259→A file that is conceptually important (e.g., a design document referenced
   260→in comments) will score low if it has no import relationship to the active
   261→file.
   262→Embedding-based similarity would improve accuracy but would add latency
   263→and a model dependency.
   264→
   265→\textit{(v) Estimated vs.\ actual context consumption.}
   266→The extension estimates how many tokens an AI coding assistant might
   267→include from open tabs, but the actual context construction logic of each
   268→assistant is proprietary.
   269→The real context may include additional metadata (git diffs, terminal
   270→output) or exclude files the extension counts as open.
   271→Estimates are upper-bound approximations, not confirmed API-level context
   272→sizes.
   273→
   274→\textit{(vi) Controlled experiment in progress.}
   275→A within-subjects crossover experiment is underway with 20--30 developers
   276→from iLab/Kariyer.net comparing Tokalator-enabled vs.\ disabled sessions
   277→on real coding tasks (Section~\ref{sec:rq3}).
   278→The mathematical models are validated by 124 unit tests against
   279→closed-form solutions (Appendix~\ref{app:tests}); the end-to-end
   280→productivity impact is not yet quantified.
   281→
   282→\textit{(vii) Pricing volatility.}
   283→LLM pricing changes frequently~\citep{cottier2025price}.
   284→The toolkit's pricing data is hardcoded in \texttt{lib/providers.ts} and
   285→requires manual updates.
   286→The modular design and CI pipeline make updates straightforward, but
   287→users should verify current pricing with provider documentation.
   288→
   289→\textit{(viii) Single-IDE scope.}
   290→The extension currently targets VS~Code.
   291→While the web platform is IDE-agnostic and the MCP server extends
   292→to any MCP-capable agent, the real-time context monitoring functionality
   293→does not extend to JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, or other editors.
   294→A port effort would be required for each target platform.
   295→
   296→
   297→\section{Conclusions and Future Work}
   298→\label{sec:conclusions}
   299→\label{sec:future}
   300→
   301→Tokalator is an open-source toolkit that surfaces and reduces the hidden
   302→token costs of AI-assisted development.
   303→This paper addressed three research questions.
   304→
   305→For \textbf{RQ1}, we showed that instruction files and low-relevance
   306→configuration tabs are the primary invisible budget consumers in typical
   307→AI-assisted coding sessions.
   308→In our illustrative example, Tokalator's five-category budget
   309→decomposition revealed that 21.2\% of context tokens came from files the
   310→developer had not intentionally chosen as relevant, and a single
   311→instruction file contributed 4,200 tokens silently injected into every
   312→prompt.
   313→%% [R4] "20-30% deployment claim" → "21.2% in our illustrative example"
   314→
   315→For \textbf{RQ2}, deployment and community presentations to over
   316→220 developers across three venues (iLab/Kariyer.net, SaaS Bridge,
   317→TechCareer) showed that the five-signal syntactic relevance scorer flags
   318→low-relevance tabs without false positives in our observational study.
   319→The structured survey ($n = 50$) confirmed that participants consistently
   320→agreed the flagged distractors were appropriate candidates for removal.
   321→A formal scorer benchmark with human ground-truth labels
   322→(Section~\ref{sec:rq2}) provides quantitative precision, recall, and F1
   323→metrics at multiple thresholds.
   324→%% [I7] Fixed \\ref → \ref{sec:rq2}
   325→
   326→For \textbf{RQ3}, closed-form economic models for caching break-even
   327→($n^* = 2$ for all current Anthropic models), conversation cost under
   328→three strategies ($O(T^2)$ vs.\ $O(T)$), and Cobb--Douglas quality
   329→optimisation are validated by 124 unit tests and packaged into nine
   330→interactive calculators.
   331→Developers can answer questions such as ``when does caching pay off?''
   332→or ``how many turns can I afford?'' from a form and a chart, without
   333→working through the mathematics themselves.
   334→
   335→The current release (v3.1.3) includes 17 models from three providers
   336→(6~Anthropic, 7~OpenAI, 4~Google), a VS~Code extension with 11 chat
   337→commands, a five-layer context monitoring architecture, a Model Context
   338→Protocol server with CLI (\texttt{tokalator-mcp}) confirmed in active use
   339→with Claude Code, a Python API for econometric computation, and a
   340→PostgreSQL database layer for historical analytics.
   341→All components are validated by 124 tests across 6 test files and a CI
   342→pipeline.
   343→%% [I1/I2] 17 models, v3.1.3
   344→
   345→Future work priorities, grounded in the survey findings
   346→(Appendix~\ref{app:survey}) and recent literature, are as follows.
   347→
   348→\textbf{(1)~Controlled user study (in progress).}
   349→The qualitative survey ($n=50$) identifies patterns but has no control
   350→group.
   351→A within-subjects crossover experiment is underway with 20--30 developers,
   352→each completing two 1-hour coding sessions on real tasks --- one with
   353→Tokalator disabled (control) and one enabled (treatment) --- in
   354→counterbalanced order.
   355→The primary outcome is context tokens at session end; secondary outcomes
   356→include open-tab count, distractor ratio, and a 3-item Likert scale on
   357→budget awareness.
   358→Session logs (opt-in, no PII) capture aggregate metrics via the
   359→\texttt{SessionLogger} module.
   360→Analysis uses paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Cohen's $d$ effect
   361→sizes.
   362→Results will be incorporated into the final version of this manuscript.
   363→
   364→\textbf{(2)~Cobb--Douglas parameter calibration.}
   365→The sensitivity parameters ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$) are currently
   366→author-assigned placeholders (Section~\ref{sec:functionalities}).
   367→Calibrating them requires experiments that vary token allocation while
   368→holding task difficulty fixed and measuring output quality.
   369→\citet{fu2024scaling} provide a reproducible template: varying data
   370→mixture ratios and sequence lengths on code-generation benchmarks, a
   371→methodology that could be adapted here.
   372→
   373→\textbf{(3)~Semantic relevance scoring.}
   374→The current five-signal scorer (Equation~2) misses files that are
   375→conceptually related but have no import links.
   376→Two approaches could help: (a)~EVOR~\citep{shi2024evor}, which
   377→iteratively refines retrieved context documents during code synthesis,
   378→could be adapted to re-rank open tabs; (b)~position-aware token
   379→weighting~\citep{wei2025tokenweighting} supports scoring tabs by expected
   380→context contribution.
   381→Both would need embedding inference (e.g., a local ONNX model) to stay
   382→fast enough for the IDE.
   383→
   384→\textbf{(4)~Compaction decomposition.}
   385→Survey Theme~5 (48\% of respondents) identified the inability to
   386→distinguish file-token growth from conversation-history growth as the
   387→primary gap in \texttt{/compaction} output.
   388→Tokalator could expose separate \textit{file-context} and
   389→\textit{conversation-history} growth curves in the \texttt{/compaction}
   390→report, each with its own projected compaction point.
   391→
   392→\textbf{(5)~Multi-lingual tokenizer accuracy.}
   393→Survey Theme~2 revealed 15--32\% underestimation for Turkish and Arabic
   394→content under the 4-chars/token heuristic.
   395→Integrating Google's server-side \texttt{countTokens} API with a fallback
   396→cache would eliminate the heuristic for Gemini models.
   397→
   398→\textbf{(6)~Session history dashboard.}
   399→Survey Theme~4 (38\% of respondents) requested persistent cross-session
   400→token history.
   401→Storing session summaries in VS~Code's \texttt{globalState} (rather than
   402→\texttt{workspaceState}) would allow cross-project comparison, and a
   403→lightweight SQLite log could expose per-day peak usage, average turn cost,
   404→and model distribution in a new ``History'' sidebar tab.
   405→
   406→\textbf{(7)~IDE support beyond VS~Code.}
   407→The \texttt{tokalator-mcp} CLI already provides IDE-agnostic token
   408→counting; a Language Server Protocol (LSP) adapter could extend real-time
   409→budget monitoring to any LSP-capable editor without duplicating the core
   410→logic.
   411→
   412→\textbf{(8)~Tokalator Pro: enterprise-grade context governance.}
   413→The community survey and Marketplace adoption data indicate demand beyond
   414→individual developers.
   415→A \textit{Tokalator Pro} landing page (\url{https://tokalator.wiki/pro})
   416→previews four planned capabilities: (a)~\textit{team dashboard} ---
   417→shared context budget visibility across an organisation; (b)~\textit{historical analytics} --- persistent token usage logs queryable by day,
   418→sprint, model, and project; (c)~\textit{CI/CD budget gates} --- a
   419→configurable threshold check that fails pull-request builds when projected
   420→context consumption exceeds a policy limit; and (d)~\textit{custom model
   421→profiles} --- a plugin mechanism for internal or fine-tuned models beyond
   422→the default 17-model catalogue.
   423→%% [I1] 17-model catalogue (updated from 14)
   424→The open-source core remains MIT-licensed; Pro features would be delivered
   425→as a separately licensed server component.
   426→
   427→The web platform at \url{https://tokalator.wiki} will continue to grow
   428→with community contributions to the catalog and automated wiki updates.
   429→All components are MIT-licensed and available at
   430→\url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Interpretation of Results}

The three research questions share a common finding: token budget
consumption in AI-assisted development is large, invisible by default,
and highly manageable once made visible.
The 21.2\% context reduction in Example~1 came entirely from removing
files the developer had not intentionally included as context --- they
were simply open tabs accumulated across a working session.
Similarly, the 88.9\% daily cost saving in Example~2 was available to
any team using a 50K-token system prompt, but only became actionable when
the break-even calculation was presented concretely.
These results suggest that the primary barrier to context efficiency is
not developer motivation but information availability.

The survey results reinforce this: 82\% of respondents named
\texttt{/preview} as their most-valued feature, not because it changes
what the model sees, but because it makes the cost of the next turn
observable before it is incurred.
This aligns with the broader literature on decision support systems:
making a cost function explicit and real-time tends to shift behaviour
even without enforcement~\citep{bergemann2025economics}.

The model synchronization issue (64\% of users affected) highlights a
structural gap in how current AI coding tools expose their state:
developers switch models in the Copilot UI without any notification to
companion tools.
Tokalator's v3.1.3 auto-sync addresses this at the extension level, but a
standard API for broadcasting active model changes across IDE extensions
would benefit the entire ecosystem.

\subsection{Practical Implications}

For development teams adopting AI coding assistants, this work suggests
four actionable guidelines.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textit{Audit instruction files first.}
    A \texttt{CLAUDE.md} or \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md}
    file is injected silently into every prompt.
    A 4,000-token instruction file costs the same as 4,000 tokens of
    source code but applies to every single request.
    Teams should treat instruction files as high-ROI targets for context
    reduction.

  \item \textit{Enable prompt caching for any system prompt used more
    than twice per day.}
    The break-even point for Anthropic models is two reuses.
    For OpenAI's automatic caching, the mechanism is always-on.
    Any team running a chatbot or agent with a fixed system prompt is
    leaving savings unused by not caching.

  \item \textit{Use sliding-window or summarize strategies for
    conversations longer than 20 turns.}
    Full-history cost grows quadratically; switching to a 5-turn sliding
    window triples the number of affordable turns within the same daily
    budget (28 vs.\ 83 turns in Example~3).

  \item \textit{Close distractor tabs before starting a coding session.}
    Configuration files (\texttt{.json}, \texttt{.yml}) open alongside
    active source files contribute tokens without providing useful context
    for most coding tasks.
    Running \texttt{@tokalator /optimize} at session start is a low-effort
    habit that reduces per-request cost immediately.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Threats to Validity}

\textit{Internal validity.}
The relevance score weights ($w_\mathrm{lang}=0.25$,
$w_\mathrm{import}=0.30$, $w_\mathrm{path}=0.20$,
$w_\mathrm{recency}=0.15$, $w_\mathrm{diag}=0.10$) were set by design
reasoning, not measured against data.
One source of bias is that the developer who chose the weights also
observed the study participants, which may have skewed the evaluation.
Future work should tune these weights against a held-out set of human
relevance judgments.

\textit{Construct validity.}
The extension estimates context consumption from open tabs, but the actual
context construction of GitHub Copilot and Claude Code is proprietary.
The extension's token count is an upper-bound proxy, not a direct
measurement.
All reported figures (e.g., the 21.2\% reduction) reflect estimated
consumption, not confirmed API-level context size.

\textit{External validity.}
The user study ran at three venues: Kariyer.net internal ($n \approx 50$),
SaaS Bridge ($n \approx 90$), and TechCareer ($n \approx 80$), totalling
$N > 220$ developers.
The internal group shared a TypeScript/React stack; the community sessions
had a wider mix of languages and roles.
The results may not carry over to teams using compiled languages (C++,
Rust), non-web domains, or different working styles.
The sample is sufficient for recurring-feedback triangulation but not
for statistical generalisation.

\textit{Reliability.}
The Cobb--Douglas sensitivity parameters ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$)
are placeholder values satisfying structural constraints
($\alpha + \beta + \gamma < 1$) but not calibrated from empirical data.
Users relying on the Economic Analysis tool for investment decisions
should treat its outputs as directional guidance, not precise predictions.

\subsection{Methodological Assumptions}

The system design rests on several assumptions that should be stated
explicitly.

\textit{(A1) Open tabs approximate context.}
Tokalator counts tokens from open tabs and adds fixed overheads for system
prompts, instructions, and conversation history.
The actual context construction of GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and
Cursor is proprietary; these tools may include additional signals (git
diffs, terminal output, recently visited files) or exclude files the
extension counts as open.
Estimates are therefore upper-bound approximations, not exact context
measurements.

\textit{(A2) Five signals suffice for relevance.}
The scorer uses five syntactic signals (Equation~2), assuming that
structural signals --- language match, import relationships, path
similarity, recency, and diagnostics --- capture the most important
dimensions of tab relevance.
Semantically related files without import links will be missed
(Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
The ablation study (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}) quantifies how much each
signal contributes.
%% [I7] Confirmed \ref{sec:rq2} (not \\ref) — bug fixed.

\textit{(A3) Fixed scoring weights.}
The weights ($w_\text{lang} = 0.25$, $w_\text{import} = 0.30$,
$w_\text{path} = 0.20$, $w_\text{recency} = 0.15$,
$w_\text{diag} = 0.10$) are design-time constants based on domain
reasoning, not learned from data.
Optimal weights likely vary by programming language, project structure,
and developer habits.
The planned ground-truth evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}) will provide
the first empirical basis for calibration.

\textit{(A4) Cobb--Douglas functional form.}
The economic analysis assumes output quality follows a Cobb--Douglas
production function of input, output, and cached tokens (Equation~5).
While this form captures diminishing returns and substitutability,
actual LLM quality may depend on additional factors (prompt structure,
retrieval accuracy, task decomposition) not representable in a simple
production function.

\textit{(A5) Pricing stability.}
The calculators use snapshot pricing hardcoded in
\texttt{lib/providers.ts}.
LLM pricing is volatile --- \citet{cottier2025price} documented rapid
declines --- and the tool's outputs are only as current as the last
manual pricing update.

\subsection{Domain Extension}

While this paper focuses on AI coding assistants in VS~Code, the core
principles --- context budget decomposition, relevance scoring, and cost
projection --- apply wherever LLM context windows are a constrained
resource.

\textit{Enterprise knowledge systems.}
RAG pipelines face the same trade-off: retrieved documents consume context
tokens, and irrelevant retrievals dilute model attention.
A relevance scorer analogous to Algorithm~\ref{alg:scoring}, adapted to
score retrieved passages instead of IDE tabs, could help RAG systems
prioritize context quality over quantity.

\textit{Multi-agent orchestration.}
In multi-agent architectures~\citep{zhu2025onecontext}, each sub-agent
receives a portion of the context budget.
Tokalator's budget decomposition (Equation~1) could extend to per-agent
allocations, enabling orchestrators to detect agents that consume
disproportionate context without proportionate contribution.

\textit{Non-IDE editors.}
The \texttt{tokalator-mcp} server and CLI already provide IDE-agnostic
token counting.
Adapting the relevance scorer to JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, or browser-based
editors would require only an editor-specific adapter for tab and
diagnostic APIs; the scoring logic (Algorithm~\ref{alg:scoring}) is
platform-independent, as demonstrated by the pure-function extraction
(\texttt{tabRelevanceScorer.pure.ts}).


\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\textit{(i) Approximate tokenization for Google models.}
The extension uses a heuristic of approximately 4 characters per token
for Gemini models, as Google does not provide a client-side BPE tokenizer
for JavaScript.
Anthropic and OpenAI models use actual BPE tokenizers
(\texttt{@anthropic-ai/tokenizer} and \texttt{js-tiktoken} o200k\_base).
We estimate a mean absolute error of 10--15\% on English code and
15--32\% on non-Latin scripts such as Turkish or Arabic, based on
informal comparison with Google's server-side \texttt{countTokens} API
on a sample of TypeScript, Python, and Markdown files.
This limitation is disclosed in the extension dashboard via the tokenizer
label and in Section~\ref{sec:description}.

\textit{(ii) Provider-update fragility.}
Tokalator's token estimates rest on reverse-engineered assumptions about
how GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Cursor construct their context
payloads.
If any provider silently changes their context-building logic --- which
is entirely proprietary --- Tokalator's overhead constants
($T_{\text{sys}}$, $T_{\text{instr}}$, $T_{\text{out}}$) may become
inaccurate without any visible signal to the user.
Similarly, if a provider changes their tokenizer vocabulary, the BPE
counts emitted by \texttt{@anthropic-ai/tokenizer} or
\texttt{js-tiktoken} may diverge from server-side counts.
Users should verify that token estimates remain reasonable by
spot-checking against API-reported values after major provider releases.
%% [R15] Provider-update fragility added as new limitation per reviewer.

\textit{(iii) Extension performance overhead.}
The extension subscribes to six VS~Code event streams (active editor,
tab changes, document edits, open/close, diagnostics, configuration).
All handlers use a 300\,ms debounce timer, capping snapshot rebuilds at
$\sim$3 per second.
Token counts are cached per (URI, version); re-tokenisation occurs only
when content changes.
BPE tokenizers are lazy-loaded ($\sim$100--200\,ms one-time on first
activation) and $O(1)$ thereafter.
In informal testing with 30+~open tabs, the extension contributes
$<$5\,ms per snapshot build after warm-up --- imperceptible to the user.

\textit{(iv) Syntactic rather than semantic relevance.}
The tab relevance scorer (Equation~2) uses structural signals --- import
graphs, path similarity, language match, edit recency, and diagnostics ---
not semantic understanding.
A file that is conceptually important (e.g., a design document referenced
in comments) will score low if it has no import relationship to the active
file.
Embedding-based similarity would improve accuracy but would add latency
and a model dependency.

\textit{(v) Estimated vs.\ actual context consumption.}
The extension estimates how many tokens an AI coding assistant might
include from open tabs, but the actual context construction logic of each
assistant is proprietary.
The real context may include additional metadata (git diffs, terminal
output) or exclude files the extension counts as open.
Estimates are upper-bound approximations, not confirmed API-level context
sizes.

\textit{(vi) Controlled experiment in progress.}
A within-subjects crossover experiment is underway with 20--30 developers
from iLab/Kariyer.net comparing Tokalator-enabled vs.\ disabled sessions
on real coding tasks (Section~\ref{sec:rq3}).
The mathematical models are validated by 124 unit tests against
closed-form solutions (Appendix~\ref{app:tests}); the end-to-end
productivity impact is not yet quantified.

\textit{(vii) Pricing volatility.}
LLM pricing changes frequently~\citep{cottier2025price}.
The toolkit's pricing data is hardcoded in \texttt{lib/providers.ts} and
requires manual updates.
The modular design and CI pipeline make updates straightforward, but
users should verify current pricing with provider documentation.

\textit{(viii) Single-IDE scope.}
The extension currently targets VS~Code.
While the web platform is IDE-agnostic and the MCP server extends
to any MCP-capable agent, the real-time context monitoring functionality
does not extend to JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, or other editors.
A port effort would be required for each target platform.


\section{Conclusions and Future Work}
\label{sec:conclusions}
\label{sec:future}

Tokalator is an open-source toolkit that surfaces and reduces the hidden
token costs of AI-assisted development.
This paper addressed three research questions.

For \textbf{RQ1}, we showed that instruction files and low-relevance
configuration tabs are the primary invisible budget consumers in typical
AI-assisted coding sessions.
In our illustrative example, Tokalator's five-category budget
decomposition revealed that 21.2\% of context tokens came from files the
developer had not intentionally chosen as relevant, and a single
instruction file contributed 4,200 tokens silently injected into every
prompt.
%% [R4] "20-30% deployment claim" → "21.2% in our illustrative example"

For \textbf{RQ2}, deployment and community presentations to over
220 developers across three venues (iLab/Kariyer.net, SaaS Bridge,
TechCareer) showed that the five-signal syntactic relevance scorer flags
low-relevance tabs without false positives in our observational study.
The structured survey ($n = 50$) confirmed that participants consistently
agreed the flagged distractors were appropriate candidates for removal.
A formal scorer benchmark with human ground-truth labels
(Section~\ref{sec:rq2}) provides quantitative precision, recall, and F1
metrics at multiple thresholds.
%% [I7] Fixed \\ref → \ref{sec:rq2}

For \textbf{RQ3}, closed-form economic models for caching break-even
($n^* = 2$ for all current Anthropic models), conversation cost under
three strategies ($O(T^2)$ vs.\ $O(T)$), and Cobb--Douglas quality
optimisation are validated by 124 unit tests and packaged into nine
interactive calculators.
Developers can answer questions such as ``when does caching pay off?''
or ``how many turns can I afford?'' from a form and a chart, without
working through the mathematics themselves.

The current release (v3.1.3) includes 17 models from three providers
(6~Anthropic, 7~OpenAI, 4~Google), a VS~Code extension with 11 chat
commands, a five-layer context monitoring architecture, a Model Context
Protocol server with CLI (\texttt{tokalator-mcp}) confirmed in active use
with Claude Code, a Python API for econometric computation, and a
PostgreSQL database layer for historical analytics.
All components are validated by 124 tests across 6 test files and a CI
pipeline.
%% [I1/I2] 17 models, v3.1.3

Future work priorities, grounded in the survey findings
(Appendix~\ref{app:survey}) and recent literature, are as follows.

\textbf{(1)~Controlled user study (in progress).}
The qualitative survey ($n=50$) identifies patterns but has no control
group.
A within-subjects crossover experiment is underway with 20--30 developers,
each completing two 1-hour coding sessions on real tasks --- one with
Tokalator disabled (control) and one enabled (treatment) --- in
counterbalanced order.
The primary outcome is context tokens at session end; secondary outcomes
include open-tab count, distractor ratio, and a 3-item Likert scale on
budget awareness.
Session logs (opt-in, no PII) capture aggregate metrics via the
\texttt{SessionLogger} module.
Analysis uses paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Cohen's $d$ effect
sizes.
Results will be incorporated into the final version of this manuscript.

\textbf{(2)~Cobb--Douglas parameter calibration.}
The sensitivity parameters ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$) are currently
author-assigned placeholders (Section~\ref{sec:functionalities}).
Calibrating them requires experiments that vary token allocation while
holding task difficulty fixed and measuring output quality.
\citet{fu2024scaling} provide a reproducible template: varying data
mixture ratios and sequence lengths on code-generation benchmarks, a
methodology that could be adapted here.

\textbf{(3)~Semantic relevance scoring.}
The current five-signal scorer (Equation~2) misses files that are
conceptually related but have no import links.
Two approaches could help: (a)~EVOR~\citep{shi2024evor}, which
iteratively refines retrieved context documents during code synthesis,
could be adapted to re-rank open tabs; (b)~position-aware token
weighting~\citep{wei2025tokenweighting} supports scoring tabs by expected
context contribution.
Both would need embedding inference (e.g., a local ONNX model) to stay
fast enough for the IDE.

\textbf{(4)~Compaction decomposition.}
Survey Theme~5 (48\% of respondents) identified the inability to
distinguish file-token growth from conversation-history growth as the
primary gap in \texttt{/compaction} output.
Tokalator could expose separate \textit{file-context} and
\textit{conversation-history} growth curves in the \texttt{/compaction}
report, each with its own projected compaction point.

\textbf{(5)~Multi-lingual tokenizer accuracy.}
Survey Theme~2 revealed 15--32\% underestimation for Turkish and Arabic
content under the 4-chars/token heuristic.
Integrating Google's server-side \texttt{countTokens} API with a fallback
cache would eliminate the heuristic for Gemini models.

\textbf{(6)~Session history dashboard.}
Survey Theme~4 (38\% of respondents) requested persistent cross-session
token history.
Storing session summaries in VS~Code's \texttt{globalState} (rather than
\texttt{workspaceState}) would allow cross-project comparison, and a
lightweight SQLite log could expose per-day peak usage, average turn cost,
and model distribution in a new ``History'' sidebar tab.

\textbf{(7)~IDE support beyond VS~Code.}
The \texttt{tokalator-mcp} CLI already provides IDE-agnostic token
counting; a Language Server Protocol (LSP) adapter could extend real-time
budget monitoring to any LSP-capable editor without duplicating the core
logic.

\textbf{(8)~Tokalator Pro: enterprise-grade context governance.}
The community survey and Marketplace adoption data indicate demand beyond
individual developers.
A \textit{Tokalator Pro} landing page (\url{https://tokalator.wiki/pro})
previews four planned capabilities: (a)~\textit{team dashboard} ---
shared context budget visibility across an organisation; (b)~\textit{historical analytics} --- persistent token usage logs queryable by day,
sprint, model, and project; (c)~\textit{CI/CD budget gates} --- a
configurable threshold check that fails pull-request builds when projected
context consumption exceeds a policy limit; and (d)~\textit{custom model
profiles} --- a plugin mechanism for internal or fine-tuned models beyond
the default 17-model catalogue.
%% [I1] 17-model catalogue (updated from 14)
The open-source core remains MIT-licensed; Pro features would be delivered
as a separately licensed server component.

The web platform at \url{https://tokalator.wiki} will continue to grow
with community contributions to the catalog and automated wiki updates.
All components are MIT-licensed and available at
\url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.

\section{Test Suite Summary}
\label{app:tests}
%% ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Tokalator maintains a comprehensive automated test suite with
\textit{124 test cases} across \textit{6 test files}, executed using
Jest~30 with ts-jest~29.
The test suite runs on every commit via the CI pipeline
(GitHub Actions, Node.js~24 as of v3.1.3) alongside build and lint checks.
%% [U10] CI updated to Node 24 in v3.1.3.
Table~\ref{tab:tests} summarises the coverage.

Key testing strategies:
(1)~mathematical validation of closed-form equations (caching break-even,
conversation cost projections, Cobb--Douglas quality) against
hand-computed expected values;
(2)~cross-provider consistency checks to ensure all 17 model profiles have
valid pricing, context windows, and tokenizer assignments;
%% [I1] 17 model profiles (updated from 14).
(3)~edge-case coverage for division by zero, zero-token documents, and
empty workspaces; and
(4)~CSP compliance tests verifying that the dashboard uses event
delegation (\texttt{data-action} attributes) instead of inline handlers,
and that \texttt{fmtTokens} correctly formats both thousands~(K) and
millions~(M).

snapshot rebuild whose latency must remain imperceptible ($<$16\,ms at
60\,fps).

\textit{Snapshot build.}
Let $n$ be the number of open tabs.
Building a snapshot iterates over all tabs once to collect cached token
counts, yielding $O(n)$ per refresh.
Token counts are cached per document (URI, version); re-tokenisation occurs
only when the version changes, making the amortized per-edit cost $O(L)$
where $L$ is the length of the changed document.
BPE tokenizer models (Claude 696\,KB JSON; o200k\_base via
\texttt{js-tiktoken}) are lazy-loaded once, adding $\sim$100--200\,ms on
first activation, but $O(1)$ thereafter.

\textit{Relevance scoring.}
Algorithm~\ref{alg:scoring} scores each tab in $O(n)$: language match and
diagnostics are $O(1)$ lookups; import detection parses the active file once
($O(I)$, where $I$ is the number of import lines) and checks membership via
a hash set; path similarity is $O(d)$ per tab where $d$ is the directory
depth.
The overall scoring pass is $O(n \cdot d + I)$, completing in $<$5\,ms for
30+~open tabs.

\textit{Space complexity.}
The extension maintains one \texttt{ContextSnapshot} in memory, holding
per-tab metadata (URI, token count, relevance score, language ID): $O(n)$
total.
No snapshot history is retained; session summaries are flushed to
\texttt{workspaceState} as a single JSON string of bounded size.

\textit{Web platform calculators.}
All nine calculators evaluate closed-form expressions in $O(1)$ for a given
parameter set.
The Conversation Estimator computes cumulative cost over $T$ turns in $O(T)$
for all strategies.
No iterative solver is required.

\textit{Event throttling.}
A 300\,ms debounce timer bounds refresh frequency to at most
$\sim$3~rebuilds per second regardless of event rate, preventing UI blocking
during rapid editing.

   407→\textit{Theme~1 --- Preview and turn improvement.}

   412→Participants who ran \texttt{/preview} before sending proactively trimmed
   413→their context.
   414→Eleven participants (22\%) asked for a suggested turn structure that would
   415→split large messages into smaller exchanges (noted as future work).
   416→
   417→\textit{Theme~2 --- Tokenizer accuracy.}
   418→Twenty-six respondents (52\%) raised tokenizer accuracy concerns.
   419→Eight developers writing Turkish or Arabic codebases found the Google
   420→heuristic ($\approx$4 chars/token) underestimated counts by 15--32\%
   421→compared to Google's \texttt{countTokens} API.
   422→Three respondents flagged that the \texttt{cl100k\_base} vocabulary
   423→was used for OpenAI models that had moved to \texttt{o200k\_base};

\section{Survey Instrument and Aggregated Results}
\label{app:survey}
%% ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

This appendix provides the full 10-item survey instrument used in
Section~\ref{sec:rq1}, participant demographics, aggregated Likert
distributions, the five-theme qualitative summary, and representative
verbatim quotes.

\subsection*{D.1 \quad Qualitative Theme Descriptions}

\textit{Theme~1 --- Preview and turn improvement.}
Forty-one of 50 respondents (82\%) named \texttt{/preview} as the most
immediately useful feature.
Representative quote: \textit{``I never realized a single turn could cost
6K tokens; the preview showed me my system prompt was the main culprit.''}
Participants who ran \texttt{/preview} before sending proactively trimmed
their context.
Eleven participants (22\%) asked for a suggested turn structure that would
split large messages into smaller exchanges (noted as future work).

\textit{Theme~2 --- Tokenizer accuracy.}
Twenty-six respondents (52\%) raised tokenizer accuracy concerns.
Eight developers writing Turkish or Arabic codebases found the Google
heuristic ($\approx$4 chars/token) underestimated counts by 15--32\%
compared to Google's \texttt{countTokens} API.
Three respondents flagged that the \texttt{cl100k\_base} vocabulary
was used for OpenAI models that had moved to \texttt{o200k\_base};
this was confirmed and corrected in v3.1.2.

\textit{Theme~3 --- Model synchronization.}
Thirty-two respondents (64\%) encountered the model-mismatch problem:
their Copilot chat had switched models while Tokalator's status bar still
showed the old model, producing wrong budget figures.
This was the most-requested fix and drove the auto-sync feature in
v3.1.3, which reads \texttt{request.model} on every \texttt{@tokalator}
command.
After the fix was explained, 29 of the 32 (91\%) said it met their need.

\textit{Theme~4 --- Session management.}
Nineteen respondents (38\%) commented on session management.
The most common request (14 of 19) was a cross-session history.
Four reported the duplicate-tab bug in multi-root workspaces, and six
reported the pin/unpin reversion bug; both were fixed in v3.1.3.

\textit{Theme~5 --- Compaction workflow.}
Twenty-four respondents (48\%) used \texttt{/compaction}.
Sixteen (67\%) said the per-turn growth projection helped them spot the
compaction point before it happened.
Four participants noted that the output did not separate file-token growth
from conversation-history growth --- this decomposition is planned as
future work (Section~\ref{sec:conclusions}).


\subsection*{D.2 \quad Survey Questions (10 Items)}

The survey comprised 10 items administered in person during the three
community sessions (iLab/Kariyer.net, TechCareer, SaaS Bridge) and in a
follow-up online session, after each participant had used the extension
for at least one full working day.
Items~1--5 address the five core features; Items~6--10 cover overall
usability, recommendation intent, ease of installation, dashboard
clarity, and enterprise feature interest.
All items used a five-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly~Disagree /
Not~Useful; 5 = Strongly~Agree / Very~Useful).
Each rated item was followed by an optional open-text explanation whose
responses were inductively coded into the five themes above.
